cards.source_text: Fewer and Fewer Students Earn Degrees in the Humanities。20 years ago, nearly 15% of the undergraduate degrees conferred in the United States were in the humanities. As of 2025, that percentage is down to 8.1%. These figures are from a recent report by Humanities Indicators, a project of the American Academy of Arts & Sciences. Here are the numbers: In 2025, the nation’s colleges and universities awarded 164,847 bachelor’s degrees in the humanities—the smallest number of degrees awarded since 1991 and 30.4% below the recent high-water mark in 2012… That decline includes a particularly sharp drop of 12.7% from 2021 to 2023, followed by a more modest drop of 2.1% from 2023 to 2024, and a further decline of just 0.4% from 2024 to 2025—the smallest year-on-year decline since 2012. And most disciplines within the humanities have shown a decline: Within the humanities, almost every discipline awarded fewer degrees in 2025 than 13 years earlier… The largest proportional drops in degrees awarded occurred in religious studies (down 56.3%), area studies (53.2%), languages and literatures other than English (50.8%), English (43.8%), history (40.6%), classical studies (39.4%), and comparative literature (31%). Only three disciplines showed increases—folklore (where the small number of degrees awarded makes the numbers highly volatile), the study of the arts (with a modest 2.1% increase since 2012), and interdisciplinary humanities disciplines (where the increase was largely due to the addition of a substantial number of new programs, such as digital humanities, in the Department of Education’s 2020 revision of its Classification of Instructional Programs). How’s philosophy doing? Well, after a slight decrease last year, there has been a slight increase: In 2024, 5,763 students earned philosophy BAs. In 2025, that number was 5,918. The full report from Humanities Indicators is here. The post Fewer and Fewer Students Earn Degrees in the Humanities first appeared on Daily Nous .

cards.source_text: In 1979, the government asked Wilfred Cockcroft, a now largely forgotten maths lecturer from the University of Hull, to write a report about a crisis in the teaching of his subject to children. It was wide-ranging and meticulous, and included a chapter on a technological innovation that was suddenly becoming available to the average consumer: the calculator. Many parents and teachers feared that the gadget would undermine a basic skill and a pillar of education – one of the sacred three Rs – producing generations of dumbed-down drones who could reach for a device in their pockets to avoid the hard graft of arithmetic. But Cockcroft didn’t see it that way. Instead, he proposed embracing rather than fearing the calculator. Students should be taught with and without one – and tested accordingly. “Cockcroft is unwilling to pretend that the oncoming wave of technological progress can be dodged,” economist Daniel Susskind writes in his urgent new book. A former Downing Street policy wonk who is now also a researcher at the Institute for Ethics in AI at Oxford University, Susskind casts himself as the Cockroft of the 2020s. In an era of confusion and hand-wringing (if not outright panic) about the implications of AI, he makes the technologist’s case for breathing, learning and grasping the opportunities it presents. The maths comparison only goes so far, of course; even accounting for the hubris of the AI industry, its achievements have already wrought changes that now make the calculator seem about as consequential as the corkscrew. But while the scale of the disruption is new, the historical context is, to some extent, reassuring. The book’s title neatly taps into the techno-angst of the modern parent about a future of extreme uncertainty. If traditionally we passed down wisdom with an open-minded but fairly clear sense of how it might apply to a new generation, “today, it feels like that sense of continuity has broken. In truth, we cannot be sure the advice we gave our children last year still works for the next.” Susskind, a father of young children himself, tries to anticipate a future of artificial general intelligence (AGI) – when AI will outperform us at every economically useful task. (We now have access, via ChatGPT, Claude and the like, to what’s known as artificial narrow intelligence: systems that are good at performing specific tasks.) The following guest post is by Paul McKee (Duke), Khaoula Boulhadi (Southern Connecticut State), Helena Weymouth (College of Charleston) & Thomas Nadelhoffer (College of Charleston), the authors of the study (“Thinking Differently: Neurodivergent Traits and Responses to Thought Experiments in Philosophers and the General Population“). cards.source_text: It’s an ungainly word for English speakers, which is maybe why we do not hear it often: Gleichschaltung. Yet the concept remains central for a clear view of what happened to Germany in the 1930s. In 1933, the nation completely transformed, seemingly overnight, through “a concerted policy of ‘coordination’ (Gleichschaltung),” the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum writes. “Culture, the economy, education, and law all came under Nazi control.” Those artists and organizations that were not purged had their essential character changed to reflect an entirely different set of artistic and political values. One publication, especially, serves as an example of the Nazification of culture. The arts journal Jugend (Youth), writes Messy Nessy Chic, “had been turned largely into propaganda” between 1933 and 1940, its final year. But prior to the regime’s takeover, Jugend showcased the most avant-garde, “degenerate” artists of the era, and might have been “the ‘brainiest’ periodical of the day,” as one critic wrote in a 1904 issue of The Yale Literary Magazine. “There is no magazine published in England or in this country which is at all like it.” You can take a look yourself—browse, search, and download hundreds of scanned issues of Jugend at the University of Heidelberg’s digital archive, thousands of pages in PDF form, spanning the magazine’s forty-four-year history. You can also see images at Flickr. As in England, France, Austria, and the U.S., the Art Nouveau movement in Germany emerged from a whirlwind of post-Impressionist painting, Orientalist motifs, folk art, modernist art and advertising, book illustration, and graphic and industrial design. Appropriately, given its perch on the threshold of a new century, Art Nouveau looked both backward—to the medieval, gothic, and Romantic—and forward toward a more modernist, urbane, and urbanized sensibility. So influential was Jugend that Art Nouveau in Germany became known as Jugendstil. The Oxford Critical and Cultural History of Modernist Magazines writes, “Among Jugend’s most important qualities—indeed, an essential aspect of Art Nouveau and its German equivalent Jugendstil—was its brilliant escapism.” Founded in 1896 by writer Georg Hirth, the magazine was “from the start a venue to promote the new cultural Renaissance without recourse to the established ‘vintage’ art.” (See its very first cover right above.) cards.source_text: Frank Lloyd Wright was often strapped for cash. In that respect, he had something in common with Vincent van Gogh, who passed most of his much shorter life in more dire circumstances. Unlike Wright, who enjoyed decades of fame at the pinnacle of the American architectural profession, van Gogh remained practically unknown until after his death. But if they’ve encountered one another in the afterlife, they’ve certainly discussed one subject above all others: their shared appreciation for Japanese woodblock prints. Here on Open Culture, we’ve previously featured the collection of 500 such works of art that van Gogh left behind. At the end of Wright’s life in 1959, he owned about 6,000, many of which his estate had to sell to pay both Japanese art dealers and American tax collectors. We could say that Wright died as he lived, advanced age having not evidently diminished either his financial recklessness or his obsession with ukiyo‑e. The masters of that classical “art of the floating world” like Hokusai and Hiroshige were among his favorite artists of any kind. When still a teenager, Wright went to work for the architect Joseph Silsbee, who’d built a chapel for his uncle. “Silsbee’s cousin, Ernest Fenollosa, happened to be the world’s leading Western expert on Japanese art at the time,” writes Kevin Nute at The Conversation. It isn’t certain how well the young Wright knew Fenollosa — or indeed when he began collecting ukiyo‑e, writes Frank Lloyd Wright and the Art of Japan author Julia Meech-Pekarik, though he may have seen both Hokusai and Hiroshige’s works at the World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago in 1893, “about the time he opened his practice in Oak Park.” Eight years later, “Wright made his first voyage to Japan in pursuit of prints, and he did indeed return with enough expertise to stage an exhibition of his own Hiroshige collection at the Art Institute of Chicago in March of 1906.” He returned for two months in 1913, making it clear that he was only interested in using that time to acquire more prints. cards.source_text: The weirdest song in the entire Beyoncé catalog might just be “Daddy,” the tender finale to her massive 2003 debut album, Dangerously in Love. Originally a hidden track, for good reason, the hook of the piano ballad goes like this: “I want my unborn son to be like my daddy/I want my husband to be like my daddy.” Yeah, the Knowles fam was tripping. The “Daddy” lyrics might give you the heebie jeebies, but the real problem is that, over 20 years later, I still can’t tell if it was a song Beyoncé actually wanted to make or one she felt she had to. I know, I know, Dangerously in Love has got a few heaters on there—the go-go bounce of “Crazy in Love” and the flirtatious dancehall duet “Baby Boy” with Sean Paul, both No. 1 hits, immediately come to mind—but for an album she had been waiting all of her life to make, it’s full of artistic compromise. For as long as Beyoncé has been in the spotlight, the media has been trying to psychoanalyze her relationship with her pops, Mathew Knowles. Before his life goal was to turn Beyoncé into a massive pop sensation, he was purportedly the number-one sales rep in the medical division of Xerox. He brought that acumen into the management of his daughter’s career. As the business man behind Destiny’s Child throughout their lifespan—from a teenage foursome dropping wise-beyond-their-years female empowerment anthems to the trio that has become canon (Bey, Kelly, Michelle)—his old-school helicopter parent tendencies have been heavily documented: making them practice singing while jogging and rewatching tapes of the pop stars before them like a quarterback with Heisman Trophy dreams. His meddling and favoritism has also long been rumored to be the reason for the group’s musical chairs around 1999’s The Writing’s on the Wall, the album that stamped them as one of the great R&B groups of their era. No score yet, be the first to add. You’ll never find it said explicitly, given how Beyoncé has been media-trained since elementary school, but it was apparent that there was immense pressure on her not just to become a star, but to do so on her dad’s terms. cards.source_text: I blinked too fast, and all of a sudden, it was time to do retrospectives on the music of Young Thug. After briefly confronting my own mortality—Barter 6 and “2 B’s (Danny Glover)” are how old?—it’s staggering to consider just how large the YSL head honcho’s musical and cultural footprints are. Heads were using terms like “post-text” to describe the way his voice landed on people’s eardrums back in 2016, and there isn’t another rapper alive whose excitable flows and vocal tics could be credited with both reshaping Atlanta rap and inspiring Elton John. Even at what’s arguably the nadir of his popularity post-RICO trial, Thug is currently shepherding his second cohort of young Atlanta upstarts like Tezzus, diamond*, and Pz’ into the spotlight. skaiwater isn’t part of that clique and wasn’t even born on this side of the globe, but their frenetic, lovelorn chortles and rap-first genre-hopping mark them as a child of Thug regardless. Their breakout album, 2024’s #gigi, best showcases the ambition of an artist blending rage rap, Jersey club, and emo rock with the excitement of a kid trying to mix all the Fun Dips into one flavor. That ambition also caused wonderful, their attempt at making a Capital-A Album, to collapse under its own weight. Now they’re back with femme fatale, a leaner, Thug-inspired—lead single “HITUNES” is named after Thug’s shelved debut—bout of Pan-Africanist musical fusion. No score yet, be the first to add. From the start, skaiwater’s aesthetic relied on shocking musical contrasts. Rage distortion layered over shimmering bells and synths? Swag-era 808s chased with blasts of scrambled pop and a confetti canon? skai had you covered and, most likely, stunned. That novelty’s worn off a bit over the past two years, but femme fatale represents both a recalibration and an expansion. Genre-smashing collabs still abound—opener “vampires, zombies” finds room for twee choral vocals, guitar shredding, and DS2-era siren tags—but on femme fatale the Caribbean riddims and Afrobeats grooves, mere flirtations before, are foregrounded more than ever. “ella” and “radar, radar” skew closest, but about a quarter of the tracklist works that patented sway in somewhere. cards.source_text: For nearly 40 years now, Jennifer Herrema has tuned her inner antennae to the sound of the radio—or at least, the experience of listening to it. Navigating her vast discography—with Royal Trux, then RTX, and now Black Bananas—feels a lot like randomly sliding back and forth on an FM dial, where you might bounce between classic-rock fist-pumpers, retro roller-rink jams, crackly country golden oldies, and whatever weird shit the overnight DJ at your local campus station can get away with playing at 3 a.m. The first Black Bananas album in 12 years exists in that space beyond the city limits where the signal starts to fade, faint transmissions of bygone pop hits dissolve into static, and rock gods become ghosts. Though it was long delayed by a combination of factors (including Royal Trux’s ill-fated late-2010s reunion and the pandemic), Bad Bunch feels like the logical next step for the project—which is to say it continues to push the group toward the illogical. No score yet, be the first to add. On 2012’s Rad Times Xpress IV and 2014’s Electric Brick Wall, Herrema and bandmates Brian McKinley and Kurt Midness triggered an increasingly chaotic soundclash between two oft-segregated ’80s aesthetics: hotwired-Camaro hair metal and block-party electro. But where Black Bananas retained the ripped-denim facade of a rock group even in their most techno-curious moments, Bad Bunch dives deep into a B-boy bouillabaisse of hip-hop, R&B, dub, and pawn-shop electronics, blurring the line between experimental band and production team. This is a strange group that only gets stranger the closer it veers to pop music. In the hands of a typical band, the opening “Nutrageous & Jam” might come off as a candlelit R&B boudoir ballad primed for Lite FM rotation. Black Bananas make it feel like you’re walking through a dream where the surroundings feel familiar, but the faces are blurred and you can’t understand what anyone’s saying. Herrema stumbles and mumbles her way into the track as if she’s just been roused from a years-long nap—perhaps fittingly, given that her band has been out of commission for over a decade—but instead of shaking off the grogginess, she lingers in that half-awake state, her vocals smeared into a brassy blare that fills the space where the soft-rock sax solo would go. cards.source_text: At 18, she was one of the older girls in the cast. She could dance—in heels, no less; the importance of teenagers being able to dance in heels was often stressed. She could capably carry a tune. And she knew her camera. Adéla Jergová arrived at The Debut: Dream Academy as a day-one frontrunner. The competition show, a joint brainchild of K-pop corporate giant HYBE and American label Geffen, resulted in the formation of KATSEYE and was later re-edited into a Netflix series called Pop Star Academy. It’s reality TV with the last coat of varnish stripped: Where the producers of, say, RuPaul’s Drag Race might craft a narrative intended to signal “this person is an underdog,” Pop Star Academy straight-up labeled some of its contestants “The Underdogs.” “Adéla brings a level of professionalism that we don’t have in anyone else,” we’re told early on, and when she’s eliminated in the first round of the “survival” portion, it’s with the caveat, “We see Adéla as a solo artist.” That may go down as the luckiest rejection of her career. One of the cleverer things about ADÉLA’s full-length debut, where cleverness is in vanishingly short supply, is its title. It’s PRIMA as in “first”—first dancer, first place, first elimination. One word contains the whole ADÉLA creation myth: her ambition, her apostatic setback, and her subsequent renewal, a baptism in Manic Panic. “Ain’t in LA,” one of the record’s singles and, now, ADÉLA’s first Billboard hit, is a rich lore drop for the initiated fan. She sings of hand-me-down clothes and pop music posters smuggled into communist Czechoslovakia. “I’d rather be a nobody than to be like anyone,” ADÉLA vows, with all the stacked-vocal conviction of the early-2010s Western pop that once blared from her childhood bedroom. It’s a bleak, almost tragic coda for an album that could well make her a star, at the cost of making her unremarkable. No score yet, be the first to add. cards.source_text: Not all of us can afford beachfront property with a convertible Bugatti to match, but thanks to the new album by Argento, we no longer need to. Inspired by the riches of the Tuscan coast, Miraggi is as sultry as music tagged “Balearic” gets. Breathy flutes wisp up and down, casting their ocean spray as they pass. Lithe basslines sway against windswept chimes, beckoning you to leave it all behind. New age, downtempo, and jazz fusion shimmer and swirl together like crisp white wine. That’s right, don’t resist. Summer never has to end. If this all seems like fantasy, it’s just as much of one for Argento. The side project was conceived by German-Italian producer David August, who spends most of his time hovering between the orbits of neoclassical ambience and brainy, headphone-ready dance music. He’s performed his work at the Barbican, been interpreted by the likes of Flora Yin-Wong, Valentina Magaletti, and Claire Rousay, and operates his own experimentally minded 99CHANTS label. Basically, he’s a serious artist, the kind who works with symphony orchestras in Berlin and gets commissioned to do audiovisual installations at MUTEK. He certainly doesn’t make music that you’d expect to hear sweaty and sea-soaked between salty bites of focaccia genovese. No score yet, be the first to add. But for August, Miraggi is actually a homecoming of sorts. Born in Hamburg but having spent part of his childhood in a small mountainside town outside Rome, August pieced Miraggi together between Berlin and the Tyrrhenian coast alongside percussionist Lorenzo Setti while submerged in a haze of Italian library music from the ’70s and ’80s. The results are a kind of idealized version of Mediterranean chill-out music—the same idyllic landscape producer Young Marco envisioned in what he christened “Italian dream house” on his classic 2017 compilation, only less explicitly oriented toward the club here. These tracks ooze kitsch, but get all the details just right, reaching a swagged out nirvana as August crystalizes this luxurious and extremely specific aesthetic. Though August doesn’t completely abandon his dancefloor instincts, he primarily channels them through his continuous sense of forward motion, as Miraggi’s undulating rhythms are more likely to produce stoney-eyed nods than anything close to an Ibiza-ready drop. cards.source_text: In some rare cases, adaptations and interpretations of a literary work can surpass the source. Despite hundreds of valiant efforts on the part of fans, filmmakers, game/toy designers, and radio producers, this has never been true of the fully-realized fantasy world in J.R.R. Tolkien’s The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings trilogy (not that it’s ever been anyone’s intent). As we noted in a previous post, Tolkien’s fictional world is so intricate, its sources so vast and varied, that Corey Olsen, “The Tolkien Professor,” has made it his entire life’s work to open that world up to students and curious readers, such as with his eight-part lecture series on The Hobbit. One might also add illustrators to the list of Tolkien interpreters above who have—in the almost ninety years since The Hobbit’s publication and more than seventy years since the first appearance of The Lord of the Rings trilogy—done their best to visualize Tolkien’s world. But perhaps no one did so better than the master himself. Long known as a visual artist as well as a literary one, Tolkien left behind over 100 illustrations for The Hobbit, one of which adorns 2011’s HarperCollins 75th anniversary edition of the book. He also created these original cover designs for each book in The Lord of the Rings trilogy. In the long and complex publication history of Tolkien’s most famous of works, it’s unclear if these designs ever made it onto books published during his lifetime, but the sigil in the center of The Fellowship of the Ring design (above), with its ominous eye of Sauron surrounded by elvish runes and topped by the one ring, did grace the elegant, minimalist covers of the first edition of the trilogy. Tolkien’s artwork received a thorough treatment in a 1995 monograph J.R.R. Tolkien Artist & Illustrator, which covers over 60 years of Tolkien’s life as an artist, and the magic of flickr brings us this compendium of Tolkien illustrations. Note: An earlier version of this post appeared on our site in 2013. There, he was immediately surrounded by a crowd of people, who begged him to help one of their neighbours. And so, dismounting from his horse, he went to the man’s house, where he was confronted by the disturbing sight of a possessed man ‘lying prostrate with his head tied to a post and each of his hands to great stakes fixed in the ground.’ Despite these restraints, the man constantly writhed around, rolling his eyes, gnashing his teeth, and sticking his tongue out. To Hugh, as to the local onlookers, the diagnosis was clear: this unfortunate sailor had been possessed by a demon and could be cured only by an exorcism. Once the necessary rituals were performed, he was ‘delivered from the demon [and] … after living devoutly for some years, finally made a good and peaceful end.’ For Hugh’s biographer, Adam of Eynsham, the incident was worth recounting because it demonstrated not only that the future saint had healing powers, but that he was a brave and compassionate man (in sharp contrast to the local bishop, who had ‘galloped away as if pursued by the Furies’, rather than face a possessed man). But, to us, the story – full of fear, cruelty and superstition – sums up both everything that was wrong with medieval attitudes to mental illness, and the apparent uselessness of medieval medicine in the face of serious illness. And yet, as is so often the case when studying the distant past, the reality was rather more complicated. Influenced by stories of demonic possession (and there are lots of them, especially in saints’ lives and miracle collections), I long assumed that our ancestors’ attitudes to, and experiences of, mental health were completely different to our own – and that they would have little sympathy with our fast-growing mental health crisis. But when I turned my attention away from religious texts, and began to research medieval ideas about healthy living, I soon came across medieval people who discussed mental health in ways that felt far more familiar to me. The similarities were particularly apparent in medical writings, which outline a sophisticated argument that mental wellness was at the heart of a healthy lifestyle. cards.source_text: ‘The land had its own stories.’ A common narrative among European settlers was that the lands they occupied were empty and, therefore, free to claim. This assumption, imposed across many colonies, severed Indigenous peoples from places to which they held deep cultural and spiritual ties. Central Australia was no exception: the doctrine of ‘terra nullius’, used to justify British claims over Australia, treated the land as if it belonged to no one, disregarding the long histories of Aboriginal communities who had been living there for tens of thousands of years. For this short documentary, the British artist Patrick Waterhouse collaborated with the Warlukurlangu art centre to revisit that history by intervening in official colonial documents and maps. Working for several years with Warlpiri artists from Yuendumu and Nyirripi, he invited them to respond to these archival materials through their own visual languages. The film captures the collaborative process, the conversations prompted by these documents and the striking works that emerge: pieces in which colonial cartography intersects with Indigenous knowledge and art.

BANJARMASIN, Indonesia — Siti Sarah slept in fits and starts through August as the fires broke out around her village and surrounding peatlands. One fire on Aug. 18 at first seemed a safe distance away, but in a heartbeat the flames were within 100 meters (330 feet) of her home in Pengayuan, a village in Indonesia’s South Kalimantan province. “The fire seemed to leap up,” Siti told Mongabay Indonesia. “All of a sudden it was right there — it grew so fast.” Cries for help echoed around the village as Siti joined the community’s firefighting press. “I also helped put out a fire,” she said. “By whacking it with a piece of wood.” Two days later, firefighters scrambled to extinguish yet another blaze in the village grounds, dousing the flames before they could reach any homes. Across Indonesia, community and government firefighters have been battling fires like this since the main dry season began in July, many of them burning across carbon-rich peatlands in the low-lying deltas and plains of Borneo and Sumatra. In recent decades, Borneo’s peatlands have been drained for oil palm plantations to meet rising global consumer demand for palm oil. Fire is often used as a cheap way to clear land, but the flames can quickly run out of control across drained peatlands, which become a tinderbox when desiccated by El Niño-fueled drought. In western Borneo, animal rescuers are scrambling to save orangutans stranded by the fires, while smoke blankets towns and villages across the island, sickening residents and upending daily life. Southeasterly winds have carried smoke from Indonesia’s wildfires across borders into Malaysia and Singapore, prompting health advisories in both countries. cards.source_text: The late actor Diana Rigg declined to call herself a feminist, noting: “Why would I burn my bra? I need my bra.” Nonetheless, her ideas on womanhood were ahead of their time. In an interview with Michael Parkinson, she observed how marriage was “all rather pagan, don’t you think? … A lot of women see it as security. Well, I’m not a woman who yearns for security.” Taking over from Honor Blackman as the high-kicking Emma Peel in the 1960s spy series The Avengers, Rigg refused to play subordinate sidekick to Patrick Macnee’s Steed, turning her character into a beacon of female empowerment. When Rigg learned that not only was Macnee paid significantly more than she was, but the camera operator was too, she demanded a raise. She got it, but that didn’t stop the press from labelling her as a grasping diva. Fifty years later, she told Newsnight: “Equal pay. That’s what feminism means to me, only that.” On the stage and screen, Rigg specialised in fierce, complicated women: Medea, Phèdre, Mother Courage, the wimple-clad Olenna Tyrell in Game of Thrones. Yet in life she refused to take herself or her job seriously. Her fear of appearing earnest led her to decline offers of a biography. Now, six years after her death from cancer, her daughter, the actor Rachael Stirling, has taken on the task of documenting Rigg’s life. All About My Mother is a funny, intimate, often joyous and beautifully written eulogy to a woman who didn’t suffer fools yet remained blithely self-mocking and down to earth. Asked what it meant to be made a dame, she replied: “I think it means I’m not supposed to say ‘fuck’ anymore.” Blending memoir and biography, Stirling builds a portrait based on her own recollections, plus research into Rigg’s performances, writings, recorded interviews and press cuttings collected and stashed in a trunk by her late grandmother Beryl. The book, Stirling says, “is not a detached narrative … This is what I know, what she said, what I’ve learned, what I want to write, what she wrote and what I think she wouldn’t mind my telling you.” Wild anecdotes of stars behaving badly include the time Rigg was lured to Benny Hill’s house with the promise of a party, only to find she was the sole guest. When he appeared in the garden proffering a drink and a semi-erect penis, Rigg turned away, shouted “LOOK! PARSLEY!” and scarpered. cards.source_text: ‘She let me feel normal’ What I appreciated most about Gloria was she let me feel normal. I graduated in engineering as one of three women in a class of over 150. In her world, a feminist was a woman that wanted to be judged for her capabilities and not her gender. She was very inspirational and empowering when I first read her books as a young engineer. Teresa, Switzerland ‘A stalwart in my life’ She was a stalwart in my life and my evolution as a feminist and a supporter of the rights of women. I met Gloria Steinem once, at the very beginning of her career and of my own. Fresh out of Wellesley College, I travelled with a friend, another aspiring journalist, to cover the World Festival of Youth and Students, held in Vienna in the summer of 1959. The festival, it was widely acknowledged, was sponsored by the Soviet bloc; it came in the wake of the failed Hungarian revolt against communism and attracted young people from all over the world. From the US, there were two delegations, one called the New York group, the other the Cambridge crowd. Gloria Steinem was the super-glamorous, gorgeous, dynamic “secretary” of the Cambridge crowd. In her low-cut summer frock and what we called, even back then, “fuck-me sandals” she was a knockout, everywhere, directing operations, arranging for Ella Fitzgerald (no less) to give a free concert, feeding journalists stories, prompts, questions. I don’t think her official title was anything more than secretary, but clearly she was the person in charge. I was not surprised when she emerged several years later as a key figure in the burgeoning women’s movement. Her combination of brains and a well-nourished sense of humour brought strength, wit, and intelligence to the movement. And now, when we really need her like again, she is gone – but I pray her memory will continue to strengthen all of us who care about women’s lives and futures. items.title: How Different Are Philosophers? (guest post)
items.summary: “Do philosophers really think differently than non-philosophers?” That’s the question taken up by a team of researchers in a recent study published in Philosophical Psychology. Focusing on differences between philosophers and non-philosophers in regard to neurodivergent traits and responses to thought experiments, the researchers found some support, in the aggregate, for a “yes” answer to that question. The following guest post is by Paul McKee (Duke), Khaoula Boulhadi (Southern Connecticut State), Helena Weymouth (College of Charleston) & Thomas Nadelhoffer (College of Charleston), the authors of the study (“Thinking Differently: Neurodivergent Traits and Responses to Thought Experiments in Philosophers and the General Population“). How Different Are Philosophers? by Paul McKee, Khaoula Boulhadi, Helena Weymouth & Thomas Nadelhoffer “The history of philosophy is to a great extent that of a certain clash of human temperaments [. . .] Yet, his temperament really gives him a stronger bias than any of his more strictly objective premises. It loads the evidence for him one way or the other” — William James Neurodiversity and Philosophical Intuitions In addition to being abstract thinkers, philosophers are stereotyped as being argumentative, overly self-absorbed in their own thoughts, and enjoy creating increasingly fine distinctions regarding everyday terms while imagining novel hypothetical situations and debating the conclusions they draw. More than two millennia before the modern notion of stereotypes existed, Plato used humor to poke fun at philosophers in the Theaetetus by telling a story of Thales contemplating the stars, so engrossed that he forgot where he was walking and fell down a well. items.title: Fewer and Fewer Students Earn Degrees in the Humanities
items.summary: 20 years ago, nearly 15% of the undergraduate degrees conferred in the United States were in the humanities. As of 2025, that percentage is down to 8.1%. These figures are from a recent report by Humanities Indicators, a project of the American Academy of Arts & Sciences. Here are the numbers: In 2025, the nation’s colleges and universities awarded 164,847 bachelor’s degrees in the humanities—the smallest number of degrees awarded since 1991 and 30.4% below the recent high-water mark in 2012… That decline includes a particularly sharp drop of 12.7% from 2021 to 2023, followed by a more modest drop of 2.1% from 2023 to 2024, and a further decline of just 0.4% from 2024 to 2025—the smallest year-on-year decline since 2012. And most disciplines within the humanities have shown a decline: Within the humanities, almost every discipline awarded fewer degrees in 2025 than 13 years earlier… The largest proportional drops in degrees awarded occurred in religious studies (down 56.3%), area studies (53.2%), languages and literatures other than English (50.8%), English (43.8%), history (40.6%), classical studies (39.4%), and comparative literature (31%). Only three disciplines showed increases—folklore (where the small number of degrees awarded makes the numbers highly volatile), the study of the arts (with a modest 2.1% increase since 2012), and interdisciplinary humanities disciplines (where the increase was largely due to the addition of a substantial number of new programs, such as digital humanities, in the Department of Education’s 2020 revision of its Classification of Instructional Programs). How’s philosophy doing? Well, after a slight decrease last year, there has been a slight increase: In 2024, 5,763 students earned philosophy BAs. In 2025, that number was 5,918. The full report from Humanities Indicators is here. The post Fewer and Fewer Students Earn Degrees in the Humanities first appeared on Daily Nous .

items.title: All About My Mother by Rachael Stirling review – a joyous love letter to Diana Rigg
items.summary: Beautifully written by her daughter, this is a funny and intimate eulogy to the 60s star of The Avengers who went on to specialise in fierce, complicated women The late actor Diana Rigg declined to call herself a feminist, noting: “Why would I burn my bra? I need my bra.” Nonetheless, her ideas on womanhood were ahead of their time. In an interview with Michael Parkinson, she observed how marriage was “all rather pagan, don’t you think? … A lot of women see it as security. Well, I’m not a woman who yearns for security.” Taking over from Honor Blackman as the high-kicking Emma Peel in the 1960s spy series The Avengers, Rigg refused to play subordinate sidekick to Patrick Macnee’s Steed, turning her character into a beacon of female empowerment. When Rigg learned that not only was Macnee paid significantly more than she was, but the camera operator was too, she demanded a raise. She got it, but that didn’t stop the press from labelling her as a grasping diva. Fifty years later, she told Newsnight: “Equal pay. That’s what feminism means to me, only that.” Continue reading...

items.summary: The Syrian rock hyrax depends on the fragile landscapes of the border region. Alongside other environmentalists, I have been documenting the destruction of its habitat Wars are usually measured in the number of people killed, homes destroyed and towns erased. Far less attention is paid to what happens beneath the rubble. Across southern Lebanon, repeated large-scale detonations are not only causing human tragedy by demolishing villages , they are also destroying the ancient limestone habitats that have sheltered colonies of rock hyrax for centuries. As founder and president of Green Southerners, an environmental organisation documenting the ecological effects of war in southern Lebanon, I have been helping colleagues to record the damage inflicted on forests, wildlife and fragile ecosystems across the border region. items.title: Country diary: A little garden mystery – why are the wood mice hoarding opium seeds? | Susie White
items.summary: Allendale, Northumberland: My late-flowering poppies have lit up the garden, and it’s not only me who’s taken an interest The opium poppies have now set seed, their leaves rattling like crisp packets, the vents beneath their pod lids open for the seeds to be scattered. Dotted throughout my flower borders, adding stature to the vegetable garden, Papaver somniferum is the breadseed poppy, its large, floppy petals unpredictable in colour: pale lilac, purple, pink or sometimes with fringed petals. The unexpected brings a freedom and a randomness to the garden. Those blue-grey seeds are sprinkled on bagels and bread, baked into cakes or ground as a thickener for curries, adding protein, plant fats and trace elements such as manganese. But in its unripe state this is the plant that gives opium, a two-sided drug, both medicinal and destructive as a sedative – its specific name somniferum means sleep-bringing. Continue reading...
